clinicalPearls: The commonest form of autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, caused by IgG autoantibodies that bind red cells optimally at body temperature
Haemolysis is predominantly extravascular, with antibody-coated cells removed by splenic macrophages
The blood film characteristically shows spherocytes, polychromasia and a raised reticulocyte count
The direct antiglobulin test is positive, typically for IgG with or without complement, and is central to the diagnosis
May be primary or secondary to lymphoproliferative disorders, autoimmune disease such as lupus, or certain drugs
First-line treatment is corticosteroids, with rituximab and splenectomy among the options for refractory or relapsing disease
Transfusion can be difficult because the autoantibody reacts with most donor cells and may mask an underlying alloantibody
reference.pathophysiology: Warm autoimmune haemolytic anaemia is caused by autoantibodies, usually of the IgG class, that bind red-cell membrane antigens most avidly at core body temperature. Antibody-coated red cells are recognised by Fc receptors on splenic macrophages, which remove portions of the membrane, generating spherocytes that are less deformable and are ultimately trapped and destroyed in the spleen. This predominantly extravascular haemolysis raises unconjugated bilirubin, lactate dehydrogenase and reticulocytes while consuming haptoglobin. When complement is also fixed, some intravascular haemolysis and hepatic clearance occur. The autoantibody may be idiopathic or arise secondary to lymphoproliferative disease, connective tissue disorders or drugs, and its broad specificity complicates compatibility testing.
additionalDifferentials: Cold agglutinin disease and other cold autoimmune haemolysis
additionalInvestigations: Direct antiglobulin test, characteristically positive for IgG with or without complement
Blood film showing spherocytes, polychromasia and nucleated red cells
Reticulocyte count, typically raised as a marrow response
Haemolysis markers including lactate dehydrogenase, haptoglobin and unconjugated bilirubin
Investigation for secondary causes such as lymphoproliferative disorder, lupus and relevant drugs
Careful crossmatching to detect any alloantibody masked by the autoantibody
redFlags: Rapidly falling haemoglobin with cardiovascular compromise
Inadequate reticulocyte response suggesting concurrent marrow suppression
Features of an underlying lymphoma or connective tissue disease
Difficulty obtaining compatible blood when urgent transfusion is required
reference.prognosis: Many patients respond to corticosteroids, but relapse is common and some require second-line therapy; the course and outlook are strongly influenced by any underlying secondary cause.
pitfalls: Withholding necessary transfusion for fear of incompatibility when the anaemia is life-threatening
Failing to search for an underlying lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disorder
Overlooking a masked alloantibody during compatibility testing
Attributing spherocytes solely to hereditary spherocytosis without a direct antiglobulin test
management: Start corticosteroids such as prednisolone as first-line immunosuppression to reduce autoantibody-mediated red-cell destruction
Escalate refractory or relapsing disease to rituximab, splenectomy or agents such as azathioprine, ciclosporin or mycophenolate mofetil
Supplement folic acid to sustain the brisk marrow erythropoietic response
Search for and treat an underlying secondary cause, stopping any culprit drug and managing coexisting lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease
Reserve transfusion of warmed, best-matched red cells for severe or life-threatening anaemia, warning the laboratory of autoantibody masking of alloantibodies
Give thromboprophylaxis during periods of active haemolysis
Track the full blood count and haemolysis markers over time and watch for associated immune thrombocytopenia (Evans syndrome)
Refer to haematology and escalate promptly for cardiovascular instability or a severe haemolytic crisis
